title: Maximum Subarray
problem: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (at least one element) with the largest sum and return that sum.
example: Explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum 6.
intuition: Every subarray ends somewhere. Ask: "what is the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at index i?" It is either nums[i] alone, or nums[i] glued onto the best subarray ending at i-1. You glue only if that previous best is positive; a negative prefix can only drag you down, so you throw it away and restart.
Trace on the example: running sums go -2 → (restart) 1 → -2 → (restart) 4 → 3 → 5 → 6 → 1 → 5. The maximum seen is 6.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every start and end with a running sum, O(n²). Kadane's keeps the best sum ending at each index: extend the previous run if it is positive, otherwise restart. That's O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: all negative numbers (answer is the largest single element, so initialise with nums[0], not 0); single element.
Common mistakes: initialising best = 0 (wrong for all-negative arrays); resetting cur to 0 before adding instead of comparing x vs cur + x.

Follow-ups: "Return the subarray itself" → record a tentative start when you restart, and copy start/end when best improves. "Divide and conquer?" → O(n log n) by combining left best, right best and best crossing the middle. "Circular array (LC 918)?" → answer is max(normal Kadane, total − minimum subarray), unless all are negative. 14.2
simple: Find the stretch of neighbours with the largest sum.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Fix every start index i.
Extend the end j from i to n-1, keeping a running sum.
Track the maximum running sum seen.
approaches.why: Two nested loops over start and end; the running sum avoids a third loop.
approaches.simple: Try every start and extend to the right, tracking the best sum.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep cur = best sum of a subarray ending at the current index.
For each x: cur = max(x, cur + x) (restart if the old cur was negative).
best = max(best, cur).
approaches.why: One pass, two variables.
approaches.simple: Kadane: keep the best sum ending here. If it goes negative, start fresh at the next number.

title: Jump Game
problem: You start at index 0 of nums. nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index.
example: Explanation: Jump 1 step to index 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
intuition: You do not need to know which jumps you take, only how far you could possibly get. Walk left to right maintaining reach = the farthest index reachable so far. If you ever stand on an index greater than reach, you are stuck. Every index up to reach is reachable because jumps can be any length from 1 to nums[i].
Example [3,2,1,0,4]: reach becomes 3, 3, 3, 3, and index 4 > 3, so false.
notes: Say it like this: "A DP that marks every reachable index is O(n²). But reachable indices always form a prefix, so I only need the farthest reach. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single element (already at the end → true); zeros in the middle; nums[0] = 0 with n > 1.
Common mistakes: checking nums[i] == 0 instead of i > reach; forgetting that a zero is fine if you can jump over it.
Follow-ups: "Minimum number of jumps?" → Jump Game II (next). An equivalent backward greedy: keep goal = n-1, move it to i whenever i + nums[i] >= goal; answer is goal == 0. 14.3
simple: Each number says how far you may jump. Can you reach the last index?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Dynamic programming over "can I reach index i".
steps: ok[0] = true.
For every reachable i, mark ok[i+1.. i+nums[i]] as true.
Return ok[n-1].
approaches.time: O(n · maxJump) which is O(n²) in the worst case
approaches.why: Each index may mark up to n later indices; the boolean array is O(n).
approaches.simple: Mark every index you can reach, jump by jump.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: reach = 0.
For each i: if i > reach, return false; else reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).
If the loop finishes (or reach >= n-1), return true.
approaches.why: Single pass with one variable.
approaches.simple: Keep the farthest index reachable so far. If you ever stand beyond it, you're stuck.

title: Jump Game II
problem: Same setup as Jump Game, but the last index is guaranteed reachable. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach it.
intuition: Think of it as BFS where "level k" is the set of indices reachable with exactly k jumps. Those sets are contiguous windows. Level 0 is [0,0]. From a window [l, r], the next window is [r+1, farthest] where farthest = max(i + nums[i]) over the window. Count windows until one covers n-1.
Trace [2,3,1,1,4]: window [0,0] → farthest 2 → window [1,2] (1 jump) → farthest max(1+3, 2+1) = 4 → window [3,4] (2 jumps), covers 4. Answer 2.
notes: Say it like this: "DP over min jumps per index is O(n²). Better: indices reachable in k jumps form a window, so I do an implicit BFS level by level, tracking the current window end and the farthest next reach. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: n = 1 → 0 jumps (the loop runs zero times); large jumps that overshoot the end.
Common mistakes: looping to n-1 instead of n-2 (adds an extra jump when curEnd lands exactly on the last index); incrementing jumps on every index.
Follow-ups: "What if the end might be unreachable?" → if i == curEnd and farthest <= i, return -1. 14.4
simple: Fewest jumps to reach the last index.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: DP: dp[i] = min jumps to reach i.
steps: dp[0] = 0, rest infinity.
For each i, for each j in i+1.. i+nums[i]: dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1).
Return dp[n-1].
approaches.why: Each index relaxes up to n successors; one DP array.
approaches.simple: dp: for each index, update the jump count of every index it can reach.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: jumps = 0, curEnd = 0, farthest = 0.
For i from 0 to n-2: farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).
When i == curEnd (finished the current level): jumps++, curEnd = farthest.
Return jumps.
approaches.why: Each index is scanned once; we stop at n-2 because standing on the last index needs no more jumps.
approaches.simple: Treat it like BFS levels: each jump covers a range; when you finish a range, count a jump and move to the farthest point reached.

title: Gas Station
problem: There are n gas stations on a circle. Station i gives gas[i] fuel, and going from i to i+1 costs cost[i]. Starting with an empty tank, return the starting index from which you can complete the circle once clockwise, or -1. The answer is unique if it exists.
example: Explanation: Start at 3: tank 4-1=3, +5-2=6, +1-3=4, +2-4=2, +3-5=0. Back at 3.
intuition: Two facts do all the work: 1. If sum(gas) < sum(cost), no start works. If it is >=, some start works. 2. If you start at s and run dry before reaching j, then no station between s and j can be a valid start either: you arrived at each of them with a tank >= 0, so starting there with 0 is no better. So jump the candidate straight to j+1.
That gives one pass: keep a running tank; whenever it goes negative, reset it and set start = i+1.
notes: Say it like this: "Simulating from every start is O(n²). Key insight: if I run dry at j starting from s, every station between s and j also fails, so the next candidate is j+1. Combined with 'total gas >= total cost means a solution exists', one pass gives O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: single station; total exactly equal (tank ends at 0, still valid); start can never be n when total >= 0.
Common mistakes: forgetting the global total check; trying to "wrap" the second pass (not needed).
Follow-ups: "Why don't we need to check the wrap-around part from start?" → the surplus from start..n-1 is at least the deficit of 0..start-1, because total >= 0. 14.5
simple: Drive around a circle of gas stations. Which start lets you finish the loop?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try every start s.
Simulate n steps around the circle; if the tank goes negative, fail.
Return the first s that survives.
approaches.why: n starts times n simulated steps.
approaches.simple: Try every start and simulate the trip.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: total = 0, tank = 0, start = 0.
For each i: d = gas[i] - cost[i]; add to total and tank.
If tank < 0: start = i + 1, tank = 0.
Return total >= 0? start: -1.
approaches.why: One pass; the skip-ahead argument means we never revisit a failed range.
approaches.simple: If the tank goes negative, none of the stations so far can be the start, so restart from the next one. Check total gas ≥ total cost.

title: Hand of Straights
problem: Alice has cards hand[i]. She wants to split them into groups of exactly groupSize cards, where each group is groupSize consecutive values. Return true if possible.
intuition: Look at the smallest card. It cannot be in the middle or end of a group (nothing smaller exists), so it must start a group: x, x+1,..., x+groupSize-1. Remove that group and repeat. If any required card is missing, fail.
Doing it value by value with counts is faster: if the smallest value x appears c times, then c groups must start at x, so subtract c from the counts of x..x+groupSize-1 all at once.
notes: Say it like this: "The smallest card must start a group. Simulating that with list removals is O(n²). With a count map and sorted distinct keys, I start count[x] groups at each x at once, which is O(n log n) for the sort."
Edge cases: groupSize = 1 (always true); n % groupSize!= 0 (instant false); duplicates.
Common mistakes: iterating the hash map in insertion order instead of sorted order; subtracting 1 instead of the whole count c.
Follow-ups: "Same as LC 1296 Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers" → identical code. Java alternative: a TreeMap and repeatedly take firstKey(). 14.6
simple: Can the cards be split into groups of consecutive numbers of a given size?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If n % groupSize!= 0, return false.
Sort the cards into a list.
Repeatedly take the smallest remaining card x and remove one copy each of x+1.. x+groupSize-1 by searching the list; if one is missing, return false.
approaches.why: Each removal from an array list is O(n), and we remove n cards.
approaches.simple: Repeatedly take the smallest card and remove the next groupSize − 1 numbers.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: If n % groupSize!= 0, return false.
Count each value in a hash map; sort the distinct values.
For each value x in increasing order with c = count[x] > 0: for k in 0..groupSize-1, if count[x+k] < c return false, else count[x+k] -= c.
Return true.
approaches.why: Sorting the distinct values dominates. The subtraction loop does groupSize map operations per distinct start value, i.e. O(d · groupSize) which is O(n) whenever groups are actually formed (each start consumes groupSize cards). The map holds up to n keys.
approaches.simple: Count cards; from the smallest value up, start as many groups as there are cards of that value and use up the following values.

title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
problem: You have a list of triplets. An operation picks two triplets i, j and sets triplets[j] = [max(a_i,a_j), max(b_i,b_j), max(c_i,c_j)]. Return true if you can make some triplet equal to target.
intuition: Merging only takes element-wise maximums, so values can only grow. Any triplet with some value greater than the target in that position is poison: using it would overshoot forever. Throw those away. Among the safe ones, merging all of them gives the element-wise max, which is <= target everywhere. You succeed exactly when, for each of the 3 positions, some safe triplet hits the target value there.
notes: Say it like this: "Trying all subsets is exponential. Since merging only takes maxes, any triplet exceeding the target anywhere is unusable. Merge all the rest; we succeed iff each coordinate of the target is hit by some safe triplet. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: target equals one triplet; no safe triplets; one safe triplet matching all three.
Common mistakes: marking found from a triplet that overshoots in another coordinate.
Follow-ups: "Return the minimum number of triplets to merge?" → at most 3, pick for each coordinate one safe triplet; check whether 1 or 2 suffice. 14.7
simple: Can you merge some triplets (taking the max in each position) to make the target?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Enumerate every non-empty subset of triplets.
Merge the subset (element-wise max) and compare with target.
approaches.why: 2ⁿ subsets, each merged in O(n). Only usable for tiny inputs; shown to justify the greedy.
approaches.simple: Try every subset of triplets.

e.t: a === target[0] && b === target[1] && c === target[2]
a === target[0] && b === target[1] && c === target[2]
a === target[0] && b === target[1] && c === target[2]
a === target[0] && b === target[1] && c === target[2]
a === target[0] && b === target[1] && c === target[2]

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: For each triplet, skip it if any value exceeds the target in that position.
Otherwise, for each position k where t[k] == target[k], mark found[k] = true.
Return found[0] && found[1] && found[2].
approaches.why: One pass, three booleans.
approaches.simple: Ignore triplets that exceed the target anywhere; the rest can be merged freely. Check that each target value is hit by one of them.

e.t: t[0] > target[0] || t[1] > target[1] || t[2] > target[2]
t[0] > target[0] || t[1] > target[1] || t[2] > target[2]
t[0] > target[0] || t[1] > target[1] || t[2] > target[2]

title: Partition Labels
problem: Split string s into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Return the sizes of the parts.
intuition: Once a part contains letter c, it must stretch at least to the last occurrence of c. So start a part, set end = last[s[start]], and while scanning inside the part keep pushing end out to last[s[i]]. When i reaches end, nothing inside needs to go further: cut there. Cutting as early as possible maximises the number of parts.
notes: Say it like this: "Each part must extend to the last occurrence of every letter inside it. I precompute last indices, then sweep extending end; when i hits end I cut. O(n) time, O(1) space since there are 26 letters."
Edge cases: single character; all distinct letters (every part has size 1); one letter at both ends (one part).
Common mistakes: cutting when i == last[s[i]] instead of i == end; forgetting to reset start.
Follow-ups: It is really a merge-intervals problem: each letter defines an interval [first, last]; merge overlaps and output lengths. 14.8
simple: Cut the string into as many pieces as possible so each letter appears in only one piece.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Same greedy, but compute the last occurrence of a letter by scanning the string from the right every time it is needed.
approaches.why: Each of the n positions may trigger an O(n) scan for its last occurrence.
approaches.simple: Same greedy, but find each letter's last position by scanning every time.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Precompute last[c] for all 26 letters in one pass.
Scan with start and end: end = max(end, last[s[i]]); when i == end, record end - start + 1 and set start = i + 1.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the last array has fixed size 26.
approaches.simple: Record each letter's last position. Extend the current piece to the furthest last position seen; cut when you reach it.

title: Valid Parenthesis String
problem: String s has only '(', ')' and '*'. A '*' can be '(', ')' or empty. Return true if some choice makes s a valid parentheses string.
intuition: For ordinary brackets you track one number: open count, which must never go negative and must end at 0. With stars, the open count is no longer one number but a range [lo, hi] of possible values. '(' shifts both up; ')' shifts both down; '*' widens it: lo - 1 (star as)) and hi + 1 (star as (). If hi < 0, even the most optimistic choice has too many): fail. Clamp lo at 0 because a negative count is never a legal state to continue from. At the end, valid iff lo == 0.
notes: Say it like this: "Trying all three meanings of each star is O(3ⁿ); memoising on (index, open count) gives O(n²). The greedy insight is that the set of possible open counts is a contiguous range [lo, hi], so I track just the two ends: O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: empty string (true); only stars; "*)" and "(*" (true); ")*" (false at the first char because hi < 0).
Common mistakes: not clamping lo at 0; returning hi == 0 or lo <= 0 <= hi without the clamp.
Follow-ups: "Two-stack approach?" → push indices of (and *; match) with (first then *; finally each remaining (needs a * with a larger index. O(n) time, O(n) space. 14.9
simple: Brackets plus * (which can be (, ) or nothing). Can it be valid?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Recurse through the string carrying the open count.
For '*' try all three options.
Fail if the count goes negative; succeed if at the end it is 0.
approaches.why: Three branches per star; recursion depth n.
approaches.simple: Try all three meanings for every *.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Memoise the recursion: the state is only (i, open) and open <= n.
approaches.why: n × n states, each computed once in O(1).
approaches.simple: Memoise (position, open count) or use two stacks.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: lo = hi = 0.
If hi < 0 return false. If lo < 0 set lo = 0.
Return lo == 0.
approaches.why: One pass with two counters.
approaches.simple: Track the lowest and highest possible number of open brackets as you scan.

title: Insert Interval
problem: intervals is a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start. Insert newInterval so the list stays sorted and non-overlapping (merge where needed). Return the result.
intuition: Because the input is already sorted and disjoint, the intervals fall into three consecutive groups relative to the new one: 1. Those that end before it starts (end < newStart): copy as is. 2. Those that overlap it (start <= newEnd): absorb them by widening the new interval to [min starts, max ends]. 3. Those that start after it ends: copy as is.
No sorting needed, so it is linear.
notes: Say it like this: "I could append and re-run merge intervals in O(n log n), but the input is already sorted, so I copy everything that ends before the new interval, absorb everything that overlaps it, then copy the rest. O(n) time."
Edge cases: empty intervals; new interval before all or after all; new interval covering everything; touching endpoints like [1,2] and [2,3] (they merge, since start <= e).
Common mistakes: using < vs <= inconsistently, which breaks touching intervals; mutating newInterval while also copying it.
Follow-ups: "Find the insertion point faster?" → binary search the boundaries in O(log n), but building the output is still O(n). 14.10
simple: Insert a new interval into a sorted list and merge overlaps.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Append newInterval to the list.
Sort by start.
Run the standard merge (see 14.10).
approaches.why: The sort dominates; ignores that the input is already sorted.
approaches.simple: Add it, sort, and merge everything.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Copy every interval with end < newStart.
While start <= newEnd: newStart = min(newStart, start), newEnd = max(newEnd, end).
Add the merged new interval, then copy the rest.
approaches.why: Each interval is visited once.
approaches.simple: Copy intervals that end before it, merge those that overlap it, then copy the rest.

title: Merge Intervals
problem: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the input ranges.
intuition: After sorting by start, any interval that overlaps the current merged block must come right after it, never later. So walk through in start order: if the next interval starts at or before the end of the last merged block, extend that block's end; otherwise start a new block.
notes: Say it like this: "Repeatedly merging any overlapping pair works but is cubic. Sorting by start guarantees overlapping intervals are adjacent, so one pass merges into the last block. O(n log n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: single interval; touching intervals [1,4],[4,5] merge to [1,5]; an interval fully inside another ([1,10],[2,3]), which is why we take max for the end.
Common mistakes: setting last.end = cur.end instead of max; using Integer subtraction comparator a[0]-b[0] in Java (can overflow with extreme values; prefer Integer.compare).

Follow-ups: "Intervals arrive as a stream?" → keep them in a TreeMap keyed by start and merge with floor/ceiling neighbours (LC 352). "Very large input, can't sort in memory?" → external sort, then the same pass. 14.11

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Put intervals in a list.
Find any pair that overlaps (a.start <= b.end && b.start <= a.end), replace it by its union, and restart the search.
Stop when no pair overlaps.
approaches.why: Up to n merges, each found by an O(n²) pair scan.
approaches.simple: Keep finding any overlapping pair and merging it until none remain.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort by start.
For each interval: if the result is empty or the last block ends before this start, push it; otherwise set last.end = max(last.end, end).
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the merge pass is O(n). Output (and sort) use O(n).
approaches.simple: Sort by start; each interval either extends the last merged block or starts a new one.

title: Non Overlapping Intervals
problem: Given intervals, return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest are non-overlapping. Intervals that only touch ([1,2] and [2,3]) do not overlap.
example: Explanation: Remove [1,3]; the rest do not overlap.
intuition: "Remove the fewest" is the same as "keep the most non-overlapping". That is the classic activity selection problem: always keep the interval that ends earliest, because it leaves the most room for everything after. Exchange argument: in any optimal answer, swap its first interval for the earliest-ending one; nothing breaks, because that one ends no later.
So sort by end, keep an interval if it starts at or after the last kept end, otherwise remove it.
notes: Say it like this: "Minimum removals equals n minus maximum non-overlapping set. A DP like LIS is O(n²). Greedy: sort by end and keep the earliest-ending compatible interval each time; it leaves the most room. O(n log n)."
Edge cases: touching endpoints count as non-overlapping (>=); duplicates; one interval.
Common mistakes: sorting by start and keeping the first (fails on [1,100],[2,3],[4,5]); using > instead of >=.

Follow-ups: Sort-by-start variant also works: on overlap, remove one and keep prevEnd = min(prevEnd, end). "Minimum arrows to burst balloons (LC 452)" is the same pattern with touching treated as overlapping. 14.12
simple: Remove as few intervals as possible so the rest don't overlap.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: LIS-style DP (already much better than trying all subsets).
steps: Sort by start.
dp[i] = most intervals we can keep ending with interval i = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with end[j] <= start[i].
Answer = n - max(dp).
approaches.why: Each i scans all earlier j.
approaches.simple: DP over intervals sorted by start.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort by end.
prevEnd = -infinity, removed = 0.
For each interval: if start >= prevEnd, keep it (prevEnd = end); else removed++.
approaches.why: Sort plus one pass.
approaches.simple: Sort by end and keep every interval that starts after the last kept one ends; the rest are removed.

title: Meeting Rooms
problem: Given meeting time intervals [start, end], decide whether one person can attend all meetings (no two overlap). A meeting ending at time t and another starting at t do not conflict. (LeetCode 252, premium; NeetCode has it free.)
intuition: After sorting by start, if any two meetings overlap then some adjacent pair overlaps. So sort and check intervals[i].start < intervals[i-1].end.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking all pairs is O(n²). After sorting by start, any overlap shows up between neighbours, so one scan suffices: O(n log n)."
Edge cases: empty list (true); back-to-back meetings [5,10],[10,15] (true).
Common mistakes: using <= and rejecting back-to-back meetings; checking only against the first meeting.
Follow-ups: "How many rooms are needed?" → Meeting Rooms II (next). 14.13
simple: Can one person attend all the meetings?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Compare every pair (i, j).
If a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end, return false.
approaches.why: All pairs checked.
approaches.simple: Check every pair of meetings for overlap.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort by start.
For i >= 1, if start[i] < end[i-1] return false.
Return true.
approaches.why: Sort then a linear scan.
approaches.simple: Sort by start and check each meeting starts after the previous one ends.

title: Meeting Rooms II
problem: Given meeting intervals, return the minimum number of conference rooms needed so all meetings can happen. A meeting ending at t frees its room for one starting at t. (LeetCode 253, premium.)
example: Explanation: [0,30] in room 1; [5,10] and then [15,20] in room 2.
intuition: The number of rooms needed is the maximum number of meetings happening at the same moment. Picture a timeline: each start is +1, each end is -1. Sweep in time order and track the running total; the peak is the answer.

You don't need to keep start and end paired. Sort all starts and all ends separately and merge them like merge sort: if the next start comes before the next end, a meeting begins (+1); otherwise one ends (-1). On ties, process the end first so a room is freed before it is reused.
notes: Say it like this: "Rooms needed equals peak simultaneous meetings. Checking each start time against all meetings is O(n²). Sorting starts and ends separately and sweeping with two pointers gives O(n log n). The common alternative is a min-heap of end times: sort by start, pop the heap top if it has ended, push the current end; the heap size is the answer, also O(n log n)."
Edge cases: empty input (0); back-to-back meetings share a room (ends[j] <= starts[i], note the <=); all meetings identical (n rooms).
Common mistakes: using < for ties and over-counting rooms; thinking you must keep each start paired with its own end.

Follow-ups: "Which room does each meeting get?" → heap of (endTime, roomId) plus a heap of free room ids (LC 2402 Meeting Rooms III). "Times are small integers?" → difference array over the timeline, O(n + T). This is the same problem as 14.17 Minimum Platforms. 14.14
simple: How many meeting rooms are needed?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: The peak overlap always occurs at some meeting's start time.
For each start time t, count meetings with start <= t < end.
Return the maximum count.
approaches.why: n candidate times, each checked against n meetings.
approaches.simple: At each meeting's start, count how many meetings are running.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Copy starts into one array, ends into another; sort both.
Walk the starts with i, keeping pointer j into the ends. Before placing meeting i, free every room whose end is <= starts[i] (rooms--, j++).
Then rooms++ for the current meeting and track the maximum.
approaches.why: Two sorts; the sweep is linear; two extra arrays.
approaches.simple: Sort starts and ends separately and sweep: a start needs a room, an end frees one. Track the peak.

title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
problem: You are given intervals[i] = [left, right] (inclusive, size right - left + 1) and an array queries. For each query q, return the size of the smallest interval that contains q, or -1 if none does.
example: Explanation: q=2 → [2,4] size 3; q=3 → [2,4] size 3; q=4 → [4,4] size 1; q=5 → [3,6] size 4.
intuition: Answering queries in the given order forces you to look at every interval each time. Instead, answer them offline in sorted order. As q increases: - intervals with left <= q become "started"; add them to a pool once and for all; - intervals with right < q have "expired" and will never contain any later query either.

So keep the pool in a min-heap keyed by size. For each query (in increasing order), push all newly started intervals, pop expired ones from the top, and the top (if any) is the answer. Lazy deletion works because we only care about the top; an expired interval buried in the heap is removed when it surfaces.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks every interval per query, O(n·q). I process queries offline in sorted order: push intervals as their left end passes the query, lazily pop those whose right end is behind it, and read the smallest size off a min-heap. O(n log n + q log q)."
Edge cases: duplicate queries (sorting indices handles them; each gets its own answer); a query outside every interval (-1); single-point intervals like [4,4].

Common mistakes: sorting queries in place and losing original positions; popping intervals with right <= q (should be < q, the interval still contains q when right == q); trying to delete arbitrary elements from the heap instead of lazy deletion.
Follow-ups: "Queries arrive online?" → sort intervals by size and use a segment tree / DSU "paint" over coordinate-compressed points; each point gets the first (smallest) interval covering it. 14.15
simple: For each query point, find the size of the smallest interval that contains it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each query, scan all intervals.
Among those with left <= q <= right, take the minimum size.
approaches.why: Every query checks every interval; too slow for 10⁵ × 10⁵.
approaches.simple: For each query, scan every interval.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort intervals by left. Sort query indices by query value (keep original positions for the output).
Min-heap of [size, right] ordered by size.
For each query q in increasing order: - push every interval with left <= q (pointer i only moves forward); - pop while the top's right < q; - answer = top's size, or -1 if the heap is empty.
approaches.time: O(n log n + q log q)
approaches.why: Two sorts; each interval is pushed and popped at most once (O(log n) each); the heap and index array take linear space.
approaches.simple: Sort intervals and queries. Add intervals that have started into a min-heap by size, drop the ones that already ended, and read the top.

title: Candy
problem: n children stand in a line with ratings. Give each child at least one candy, and any child with a higher rating than an immediate neighbour must get more candies than that neighbour. Return the minimum total candies.
intuition: The rule has two independent halves: "more than my left neighbour if my rating is higher" and "more than my right neighbour if my rating is higher". Satisfy each half separately with the smallest numbers possible: - Left pass: L[i] = L[i-1] + 1 if r[i] > r[i-1], else 1. - Right pass: R[i] = R[i+1] + 1 if r[i] > r[i+1], else 1.
Child i needs max(L[i], R[i]), and that is also enough for both rules. Summing those maxima is the minimum.

The O(1)-space trick views ratings as a mountain range: count lengths of increasing runs (up) and decreasing runs (down). A decreasing run of length d costs 1 + 2 +... + d extra, and the peak only needs to grow if the down slope gets longer than the up slope that reached it.
notes: Say it like this: "Repeated relaxation until stable is O(n²). The constraint splits into a left rule and a right rule; one pass for each and taking the max gives O(n) time and O(n) space. If asked for O(1) space, I count lengths of up and down slopes and add arithmetic sums, adjusting the peak when the down slope is longer."
Edge cases: single child (1); equal neighbours (no constraint, the second can get 1); strictly decreasing ratings (n(n+1)/2).
Common mistakes: in the right pass, overwriting with c[i+1] + 1 instead of max(c[i], c[i+1] + 1); giving equal-rated neighbours equal candy (not required).
Follow-ups: "Circular arrangement?" → start the passes from a global minimum rating, treating it as a valley. 14.16
simple: Give candies so higher-rated children get more than their neighbours, using the fewest candies.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Start everyone with 1 candy.
Repeatedly sweep: whenever a child has a higher rating than a neighbour but not more candies, set candies to neighbour + 1.
Stop when a full sweep changes nothing.
approaches.why: Each sweep is O(n) and up to n sweeps may be needed (e.g. strictly decreasing ratings).
approaches.simple: Start with 1 each and keep fixing violations until none remain.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Two passes (this is the answer most interviewers expect).
steps: Left-to-right: c[i] = c[i-1] + 1 when r[i] > r[i- 1], else
Right-to-left: when r[i] > r[i+1], c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1] + 1).
Sum c.
approaches.why: Two linear passes and one array.
approaches.simple: Sweep left to right for the left rule, right to left for the right rule, and take the max at each child.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: total = 1 (first child), up = down = peak = 0.
Rising (r[i] > r[i-1]): up++, peak = up, down = 0, total += 1 + up.
Equal: up = down = peak = 0, total += 1 (the chain resets).

Falling: up = 0, down++, total += 1 + down, but subtract 1 if peak >= down (the peak is already tall enough; only once down exceeds peak does the peak need an extra candy, which the formula then includes).
approaches.why: One pass with a few counters.
approaches.simple: One pass counting rising and falling runs, adding candies as the slopes go.

title: N meetings in one room
problem: There is one meeting room and n meetings given by start[i] and end[i]. Find the maximum number of meetings that can be held in the room. Only one meeting can run at a time, and a meeting can start only strictly after the previous one ends (GFG convention: start of the next must be > end of the previous). (GFG "N meetings in one room".)
intuition: This is activity selection again (same as 14.11). Always pick the meeting that finishes first: it frees the room soonest and leaves the most time for the rest. Then pick the next meeting that starts after it ends, and so on.
notes: Say it like this: "A DP over compatible meetings is O(n²). Greedy: sort by end time and keep picking the earliest- finishing meeting that starts after the last chosen one ends. O(n log n). Exchange argument: replacing the first chosen meeting by the earliest-ending one never hurts."
Edge cases: strict vs non-strict boundary (GFG uses strict >, LeetCode-style problems usually allow >=; ask!); meetings with equal end times; n = 1.
Common mistakes: sorting by start or by duration (both fail); losing original indices when the problem asks you to print which meetings were chosen.

Follow-ups: "Print the meetings chosen" → record i + 1 when taking. "Meetings have weights, maximise total weight?" → weighted interval scheduling: sort by end, DP with binary search for the last compatible meeting, O(n log n). Minimum number of 14.17
simple: Fit the most meetings into one room.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: DP over meetings sorted by start, like LIS.
steps: Sort meetings by start.
dp[i] = max meetings in a schedule ending with meeting i = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with end[j] < start[i].
Return max(dp).
approaches.why: Pairwise compatibility checks.
approaches.simple: DP over meetings sorted by start.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort meeting indices by end time (ties by original index if you need to print the order).
lastEnd = -infinity, count = 0.
For each meeting in that order: if start > lastEnd, take it (count++, lastEnd = end).
approaches.why: Sort dominates; the index array is O(n).
approaches.simple: Sort by end time and take every meeting that starts after the last chosen one ends.

title: Minimum number of platforms required for a railway
problem: Given arrival times arr[] and departure times dep[] of n trains at a station, find the minimum number of platforms so that no train waits. A train that arrives at the same time another departs needs a separate platform (GFG convention: times are inclusive). (GFG "Minimum Platforms".)
example: Explanation: Between 1100 and 1120, trains 2, 3 and 4 are all at the station.
intuition: This is Meeting Rooms II with inclusive endpoints. The answer is the maximum number of trains at the station at the same moment. Sort arrivals and departures separately and sweep: next event an arrival (and arr[i] <= dep[j], inclusive)? One more platform. Otherwise a train left; free one.
notes: Say it like this: "Answer is peak trains present at once. Counting overlaps per train is O(n²). Sorting arrivals and departures separately and sweeping with two pointers is O(n log n); pairing doesn't matter because I only count events."
Edge cases: arrival equal to a departure (<= means a new platform, per GFG); all trains at the same time (n); trains crossing midnight (not handled by the standard problem; ask).
Common mistakes: using < and under-counting on ties; sorting only one array; sorting pairs together (unnecessary).
Follow-ups: "Times fit in 0..2359?" → difference array: +1 at arrival, -1 at dep + 1, prefix-sum, take max. O(n + T). 14.18
simple: How many platforms does the station need so no train waits?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each train i, count trains j with arr[j] <= arr[i] <= dep[j] (present when i arrives, including itself).
Return the maximum count.
approaches.why: Every train compared with every other train.
approaches.simple: For each train, count how many trains are at the station when it arrives.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort arr and dep (copies, if you must not mutate input).
i = 0, j = 0, plat = 0, best = 0.
While i < n: if arr[i] <= dep[j], plat++, i++; else plat--, j++. Update best.
approaches.space: O(n) for the sorted copies (O(1) if sorting in place)
approaches.why: Two sorts and a linear merge-style sweep.
approaches.simple: Sort arrivals and departures and sweep both with two pointers, tracking how many trains are present.

title: Job sequencing Problem
problem: There are n jobs. Job i has deadline[i] and profit[i]; each job takes one unit of time and earns its profit only if finished by its deadline. Only one job can run at a time. Return [number of jobs done, maximum total profit]. (GFG "Job Sequencing Problem"; the newer GFG signature takes two arrays deadline and profit.)
example: Explanation: Do the 40-profit job at time 1 and the 20-profit job at time 2 (any slot up to 4).
intuition: Consider jobs from most to least profitable. For each, schedule it in the latest free time slot that is still <= its deadline. Why latest? It keeps earlier slots open for jobs with tighter deadlines. If no slot is free, skip the job: every slot up to its deadline is already used by a more profitable job, so swapping can't help.
The only question is how fast you find "latest free slot <= d ". A linear scan backwards is simple; a disjoint-set "pointer to the next free slot to the left" makes it nearly O(1).
notes: Say it like this: "Take jobs in decreasing profit and put each in the latest free slot before its deadline. With a backward scan that's O(n log n + n·D); with a DSU that points each used slot to the next free one on its left it becomes O(n log n)."
Edge cases: deadlines larger than n (cap them); many jobs with deadline 1 (only the best one is taken); equal profits.
Common mistakes: placing a job in the earliest free slot instead of the latest (blocks tight-deadline jobs); sorting by deadline only.

Follow-ups: "Alternative without DSU?" → sort by deadline ascending, push profits into a min-heap, and whenever heap size exceeds the current deadline pop the smallest; the heap holds the chosen jobs. Also O(n log n). This is the same idea as LC 630 Course Schedule III.
simple: Each job takes one day, has a deadline and a profit. Maximise profit.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Greedy with a linear slot scan (this is the version Striver and GFG present first).
steps: Sort jobs by profit descending.
slot[1..maxD] all free.
For each job, scan t from min(deadline, maxD) down to 1; take the first free slot, add profit.
approaches.time: O(n log n + n · D) where D = max deadline
approaches.why: Each job may scan up to D slots.
approaches.simple: Take jobs from most profitable down and put each in the latest free day before its deadline, scanning for a free day.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Same greedy, but find the latest free slot with a disjoint-set union.
steps: Cap slots at D = min(max deadline, n) (more than n slots are never needed).
parent[t] = t for t = 0..D; find(t) returns the latest free slot <= t (slot 0 means "none").
For each job by profit descending: s = find(min(deadline, D)); if s > 0, take it and set parent[s] = s - 1 (slot s now points to its left neighbour).
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; DSU finds with path compression are almost O(1) amortised.
approaches.simple: Same greedy, but Union-Find jumps straight to the latest free day.
